questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes a law from a rule?
options: A law applies only to adults, whereas a rule applies only to children and young people
A law is enforced by the group that made it, such as a club or school
A law is made by parliament or the courts and applies to everyone in the jurisdiction
A law is written down, whereas a rule is always passed on by word of mouth
questions.explanation: Laws are made by parliament (statute law) or by judges (common law), apply to everyone in the jurisdiction and are enforced by the state through police and courts. Rules are made by non-government groups such as schools, clubs and families, apply only to their members and are enforced by the group itself. Many rules are written down too.

questions.stem: A netball club bans a player for six weeks for abusing an umpire. The same player later damages the umpire's car. Which statement is correct?
options: Damaging the car is only a breach of club rules, because it followed a game
The ban enforces a club rule; damaging the car may also breach the Criminal Code
The ban is a criminal sanction, so police cannot also charge the player
The club's ban is a law because it was made by an association registered under state law
questions.explanation: A club ban is a non-legal sanction enforcing the club's rules on its members. Wilfully damaging another person's property is an offence under the Criminal Code (Qld), which the state enforces through police and courts. A club cannot impose criminal sanctions, and a registered club's rules are still rules, not laws.

questions.stem: Which is the best statement of a main purpose of criminal law?
options: To allow private individuals to resolve disputes about money without the state's involvement
To protect people and property and maintain order by setting out offences and penalties
To compensate people who have suffered loss because of another person's breach of contract
To set out the structure of parliament and the powers of the Commonwealth and the states
questions.explanation: Criminal law defines conduct that harms society, such as assault and wilful damage, and sets penalties so that people and property are protected and order is kept. Compensation for a broken contract is the role of civil law, and the structure of government is set out in constitutional law.

questions.stem: The Queensland criminal law is described as a 'code'. This means that:
options: Queensland criminal law applies only when the Commonwealth Criminal Code does not apply to the conduct
the main criminal offences and principles of responsibility are set out in one comprehensive Act
the criminal law is made only by judges, who record their decisions in a code of precedents
each offence is written in coded language that only lawyers and judges are trained to read
questions.explanation: Queensland is a code jurisdiction: the Criminal Code in Schedule 1 to the Criminal Code Act 1899 (Qld) sets out the main offences and the general principles of criminal responsibility in a single statute. In common law jurisdictions much of the criminal law is still found in judges' decisions.

questions.stem: Who drafted the Queensland Criminal Code, which came into force on 1 January 1901?
options: Sir Edmund Barton
Sir Owen Dixon
Sir Robert Menzies
Sir Samuel Griffith
questions.explanation: Sir Samuel Griffith, then Chief Justice of Queensland and later the first Chief Justice of the High Court, drafted the Code. It was enacted as the Criminal Code Act 1899 and commenced on 1 January 1901. Barton was Australia's first Prime Minister.

questions.stem: Under section 2 of the Criminal Code (Qld), an offence is:
options: a breach of a contract or duty of care that causes loss to another person
any conduct that the community considers immoral or socially unacceptable
an act or omission which makes the person liable to punishment
any act that causes harm to another person, whether or not it is punishable
questions.explanation: Section 2 defines an offence as an act or omission which renders the person doing it liable to punishment. Conduct that is harmful or immoral is not an offence unless the law makes it punishable, and breaches of contract or duty of care are civil wrongs.

questions.stem: The rule of law is the principle that:
options: parliament can pass any law it likes, because it was elected by the people
judges should decide cases according to their own sense of what is fair
people must obey the police at all times, whether or not the police are acting lawfully
everyone, including the government and its officials, is subject to the law
questions.explanation: The rule of law means that the law applies equally to all people, including those in government, and that power must be exercised according to law. It rejects arbitrary power, so neither officials nor police are above the law, and judges must apply the law rather than personal views.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Queensland legal system most directly supports the rule of law?
options: Laws are published and accessible, so people can know what conduct is an offence
Ministers may direct magistrates on how to decide cases involving government policy
New criminal offences can apply to conduct that occurred before they were made
Police may detain people indefinitely if they believe the person is dangerous
questions.explanation: For people to obey the law, it must be known and accessible; Queensland legislation is published free online. Ministers directing judicial officers would breach judicial independence, retrospective offences undermine certainty, and indefinite detention without legal authority is arbitrary.

questions.stem: A new Queensland law lets police detain any person for 48 hours without charge if an officer 'thinks it appropriate'. Which element of the rule of law is most threatened?
options: Separation of powers, because the law was made by the Legislative Assembly
Representative government, because police officers are not elected by the people of Queensland
Equality before the law, because the law applies to every person in Queensland
Protection from arbitrary power, because detention depends on no clear legal standard
questions.explanation: The rule of law requires that power be exercised according to clear legal rules that can be tested in court. A power based only on an officer's opinion invites arbitrary use. The law applying to everyone is not the problem, and parliament making laws is its proper role under the separation of powers.

questions.stem: In the Australian legal system, the judicial arm of government is responsible for:
options: interpreting and applying the law in deciding cases
making laws by passing bills through parliament
carrying out laws through government departments
enforcing laws by investigating and arresting suspects
questions.explanation: The legislature (parliament) makes laws, the executive (the Crown, ministers and departments, including the police) administers and enforces them, and the judiciary (the courts) interprets and applies them to decide disputes and criminal cases.

questions.stem: Queensland Police Service officers investigate an offence and charge a suspect, and a magistrate later decides the case. This illustrates that:
options: police and magistrates both belong to the judicial arm of government
the executive enforces the law, while the judiciary decides whether it was broken
the judiciary enforces the law, while the executive decides whether it was broken
the legislature both enforces the law and decides individual criminal cases
questions.explanation: The police are part of the executive, which enforces the law. Courts are part of the judiciary, which independently decides whether the prosecution has proved the offence. Keeping these roles separate protects an accused person from being judged by the body that charged them.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the separation of judicial power protects an accused person in a criminal case?
options: An independent court, not the government that prosecutes, decides guilt
Parliament cannot pass any law that increases the penalty for an offence
Ministers must sit in parliament and answer questions about prosecutions
The accused may choose which arm of government will decide the case
questions.explanation: Because the courts are independent of the executive, a judge or jury free from government pressure decides whether guilt is proved. Ministers answering to parliament reflects responsible government, a link between the legislature and executive, not the separation of judicial power.

questions.stem: Most criminal offences in Queensland, such as assault and wilful damage, are made by the Queensland Parliament because criminal law is mainly a:
options: concurrent power
referred power
residual power
exclusive power
questions.explanation: The Constitution does not list a general criminal law power, so it is a residual power left with the states. The Commonwealth makes criminal laws only where they relate to one of its own powers, such as importation of drugs or offences involving federal agencies.

questions.stem: Which offence is most likely to be found in Commonwealth rather than Queensland law?
options: Assaulting another person at a Gold Coast nightclub
Importing a commercial quantity of an illicit drug into Australia
Wilfully damaging a neighbour's fence during an argument
Stealing a bicycle from the bike rack outside a Brisbane shopping centre
questions.explanation: Importation of goods relates to the Commonwealth's power over trade and customs, so drug importation offences are in Commonwealth law. Damage, stealing and assault are ordinary offences under the Criminal Code (Qld), made under the state's residual power.

questions.stem: Powers that both the Commonwealth and the states may exercise, such as taxation other than customs and excise duties, are called:
options: residual powers
exclusive powers
specific powers
concurrent powers
questions.explanation: Concurrent powers are shared: the Commonwealth may legislate on matters listed in section 51 of the Constitution and the states may also legislate on most of them. If the two laws are inconsistent, section 109 makes the Commonwealth law prevail. Exclusive powers can be used only by the Commonwealth.

questions.stem: In a Queensland criminal trial, the onus (burden) of proof refers to:
options: the maximum penalty that can be imposed for the offence
the rule that a person cannot be tried twice for one offence
which party has the responsibility of proving the case
how convinced the jury must be before it can convict
questions.explanation: The onus or burden of proof is about who must prove the case; in a criminal trial it rests on the prosecution. How convinced the decision-maker must be is the standard of proof, which in a criminal trial is beyond reasonable doubt.

questions.stem: Which correctly states both the onus and the standard of proof in a Queensland criminal trial?
options: The accused must prove innocence on the balance of probabilities
The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt
The accused must prove innocence beyond reasonable doubt
The prosecution must prove guilt on the balance of probabilities
questions.explanation: The prosecution carries the onus and must prove each element of the offence beyond reasonable doubt. The balance of probabilities is the lower civil standard. The accused does not have to prove innocence, which reflects the presumption of innocence.

questions.stem: In Woolmington v DPP (1935), the House of Lords described a 'golden thread' running through the criminal law. Which principle does this phrase refer to?
options: Every accused person is entitled to a lawyer paid for by the state
Criminal laws must be passed by an elected parliament, and must never be made by judges
The prosecution must prove the accused's guilt, subject to limited exceptions
Judges must follow the decisions of higher courts in the same hierarchy
questions.explanation: Woolmington established that it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the prisoner's guilt, subject to exceptions such as insanity and statutory exceptions. This principle is part of Australian common law. Following higher courts is the doctrine of precedent, a different principle.

questions.stem: Why does criminal law set a higher standard of proof than civil law?
options: The accused in a criminal case usually has more resources than the state prosecuting them
Juries are not allowed to decide civil cases, so a lower standard is needed for judges
A conviction can lead to loss of liberty and lasting stigma, so the risk of wrongful conviction must be kept low
Criminal cases always involve larger sums of money than civil cases, so more evidence is required before a court can decide
questions.explanation: Because the state can imprison a person and a conviction carries stigma, the law accepts that some guilty people may be acquitted rather than risk convicting the innocent. The state usually has more resources than the accused, which is another reason the burden is placed on it.

questions.stem: In the adversarial system used in Queensland criminal trials, the judge's main role is to:
options: question the accused before the trial to find out what really happened
represent the victim and present the prosecution's case to the jury at the trial
act as an impartial umpire who ensures the rules of evidence and procedure are followed
investigate the offence and decide which witnesses the police should interview
questions.explanation: In an adversarial system the two parties, prosecution and defence, prepare and present their own cases, and the judge acts as a neutral umpire, ruling on evidence and directing the jury on the law. Actively investigating and questioning is a feature of the inquisitorial system.

questions.stem: Which feature belongs to an inquisitorial system rather than an adversarial system?
options: Each party chooses which witnesses to call and cross-examines the other's witnesses
A jury of citizens decides guilt after hearing arguments from both sides
Strict rules of evidence exclude material that may unfairly prejudice the accused
The judge takes an active role in gathering evidence and questioning witnesses
questions.explanation: Inquisitorial systems, used in many European countries such as France and Germany, give judges an active, investigative role. Party control of witnesses, cross-examination, juries and strict rules of evidence are features of the adversarial system used in Australia.

questions.stem: The Coroners Court of Queensland investigates the cause of a death, and the coroner can call and question witnesses. Which statement best explains this?
options: It uses an adversarial approach, because the coroner acts as an umpire between the prosecution and the defence lawyers
It is part of the executive, because coroners are appointed to enforce the Criminal Code
It uses an inquisitorial approach, because it decides guilt beyond reasonable doubt
It uses an inquisitorial approach, because the coroner actively seeks the facts rather than deciding between two parties
questions.explanation: A coronial inquest is an inquiry, not a trial between parties, so the coroner directs the investigation, which is an inquisitorial feature within Australia's mainly adversarial system. A coroner does not decide criminal guilt.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest criticism of the adversarial system in achieving just and equitable outcomes?
options: The result may depend on the skill and resources of each side's lawyers rather than on the facts alone
Judges have too much power to investigate cases themselves, which can make them appear biased to the jury
The accused is required to give evidence and answer the judge's questions at trial
There are no rules of evidence, so unreliable material is often put before the jury
questions.explanation: Because each party presents its own case, a well-resourced side may present it more effectively, and a party without a skilled lawyer may be disadvantaged. In an adversarial trial the judge does not investigate, the accused need not give evidence, and strict rules of evidence apply.

questions.stem: Which list shows the Queensland courts from lowest to highest?
options: Supreme Court, District Court, Magistrates Court
Magistrates Court, District Court, Supreme Court
District Court, Magistrates Court, Supreme Court
Magistrates Court, Supreme Court, District Court
questions.explanation: The Magistrates Court is the lowest court, the District Court is the intermediate court and the Supreme Court, with its Trial Division and Court of Appeal, is the highest Queensland court. Appeals from the Court of Appeal may go to the High Court of Australia with special leave.

questions.stem: All criminal cases in Queensland begin in the:
options: Supreme Court (Trial Division)
Court of Appeal
Magistrates Court
District Court
questions.explanation: Every criminal case starts in the Magistrates Court, which decides summary offences and many indictable offences dealt with summarily. More serious indictable offences are committed to the District Court or Supreme Court for trial or sentence.

questions.stem: An adult is charged with murder in Queensland. Which court will hear the trial if the accused pleads not guilty?
options: The Magistrates Court
The Court of Appeal
The Supreme Court (Trial Division)
The District Court
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court's Trial Division tries the most serious offences, including murder, attempted murder, manslaughter and major drug offences. The District Court tries other serious indictable offences such as rape, armed robbery and fraud. The Court of Appeal hears appeals, not trials.

questions.stem: A person is convicted of a serious offence after a trial in the District Court and believes the judge misdirected the jury. To which court would the appeal usually go?
options: The Supreme Court's Trial Division
The High Court of Australia, without leave
The Magistrates Court
The Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Appeals against convictions on indictment in the District Court and Supreme Court go to the Court of Appeal, Queensland's highest court. A further appeal to the High Court requires special leave. The Trial Division hears trials, not appeals from the District Court.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why Queensland has a court hierarchy?
options: Cases can be heard by a court suited to their seriousness, and appeals can go to a higher court
Every case must be heard by all three courts before a final decision is reached
Lower courts may overrule the decisions of higher courts when the law has become outdated
Each court applies a different body of criminal law made for that court
questions.explanation: A hierarchy lets minor matters be dealt with quickly and cheaply in the Magistrates Court while serious matters go to more senior courts. It allows appeals and supports precedent, because lower courts follow higher courts. The same Criminal Code applies in every Queensland court.

questions.stem: A Queensland law bans e-scooter riders from using phones while riding, but it is not publicised and few people know it exists. Which characteristic of an effective law does it most clearly lack?
options: It carries no specific penalty
It treats some groups unequally
It is not known to the public
It is not able to be enforced
questions.explanation: People can only obey a law they know about, so an effective law must be known to the public. The law may still be enforceable and carry a penalty. Publication and awareness campaigns help to address this.

questions.stem: A law sets a fine for littering but exempts people who earn over $200,000 a year. Which characteristic of an effective law does this most clearly fail?
options: It is not known to the public
It cannot be enforced by authorities
It has no specific penalty attached
Its penalty does not apply to all people equally
questions.explanation: An effective law carries specific penalties that apply to all. Exempting a wealthy group also breaches equality before the law, part of the rule of law, and is unlikely to be acceptable in the community. The fine is a specific penalty and littering can be enforced.

questions.stem: A law that most of the community considers unreasonable is widely ignored, and juries are reluctant to convict. Which characteristic of an effective law does it lack?
options: It was not made by parliament
It is not acceptable in the community
It is not known to the public
It has no penalty that applies to all
questions.explanation: An effective law must be acceptable to the community; when it does not reflect community values, people are less likely to obey it and enforcement becomes difficult. Being known and having a penalty do not make a law acceptable.

questions.stem: A court provides a free interpreter so that an accused who speaks little English can follow the trial. This mainly promotes equitable outcomes because it:
options: transfers the onus of proof from the prosecution to the court
removes a disadvantage so the accused can take part on a fair footing
guarantees that the accused will be found not guilty of the charge
treats the accused in exactly the same way as every other accused
questions.explanation: Equity recognises that treating everyone identically can still disadvantage some people, so extra measures such as an interpreter are provided to make the process fair. It does not affect the verdict or the onus of proof.

questions.stem: Which situation shows a tension between equality and equity in the criminal justice system?
options: A rule requiring every accused to speak for themselves would treat all alike but disadvantage those with limited English
A law setting the same maximum penalty for an offence in every Queensland court applies to all offenders alike
Prosecutors must prove every element of an offence for every accused, whatever their background
The Criminal Code applies to everyone in Queensland, including members of parliament
questions.explanation: Equal treatment means applying the same rules to everyone, but identical treatment can produce unfair outcomes for people with particular disadvantages. Equity justifies different treatment, such as interpreters, to achieve a just outcome. The other examples apply equality without any tension.

questions.stem: In the Queensland Legislative Assembly, the stage at which members examine a bill clause by clause and may move amendments is called:
options: royal assent
the second reading
consideration in detail
the first reading
questions.explanation: After the second reading debate on the bill's principles, the Assembly considers the bill in detail, clause by clause, and may amend it. The bill then has its third reading and goes to the Governor for assent. The first reading is its formal introduction.

questions.stem: Under section 14A of the Acts Interpretation Act 1954 (Qld), when a Queensland court interprets a provision of an Act it must prefer the interpretation that:
options: best achieves the purpose of the Act
is most favourable to the accused in every case
follows the dictionary meaning of every word
was preferred by a majority of members in debate
questions.explanation: Section 14A requires the interpretation that best achieves the Act's purpose to be preferred to any other. Section 14B allows courts to consider extrinsic material, such as explanatory notes and second reading speeches, in some circumstances, but members' votes are not a test of meaning.

questions.stem: Section 14B of the Acts Interpretation Act 1954 (Qld) lets a court consider extrinsic material, such as a minister's second reading speech, when interpreting a provision. In which situation may it do so?
options: Only when both the prosecution and the defence agree that the speech is relevant
When the court disagrees with the policy of the Act and wants to change its effect
When the provision is ambiguous, or its ordinary meaning leads to a manifestly absurd result
Only when the High Court has already decided the meaning of the same provision
questions.explanation: Extrinsic material may be considered to resolve ambiguity or obscurity, to avoid a manifestly absurd or unreasonable result, or to confirm the ordinary meaning. Courts interpret Acts to give effect to parliament's purpose; they cannot change an Act because they disagree with its policy.

questions.stem: A student recommends that Queensland change a criminal law. Which justification uses legal criteria most effectively?
options: The change has been proposed many times before, so it must eventually be accepted
The change would uphold the rule of law and produce more just and equitable outcomes for accused people
The change is supported by most of the student's friends and has trended on social media
The change would be popular with voters and would help the government to win the next state election
questions.explanation: A recommendation in legal studies is justified against legal criteria, such as the rule of law, justice, equity and whether the law would be effective and enforceable. Popularity, political advantage and repetition are not legal criteria, although they may affect whether reform happens.
